The paper goes in depth into current state of affairs in stated preference methods and the authors compare different approaches in analyzing a synthetic data set. The appendix (pages 112 - 117) has complete documentation for

1. Setting up the *.stan file
2. Setting up the *.R file (I'm using RStan)
3. Creating the synthetic data set in R

parts:
There weren't any errors per se, just compiler warnings
and some numerical exceptions at runtime:

Exception thrown at line 34: lkj_corr_log: y is not positive definite. 9
Exception thrown at line 40: multi_normal_log: LDLT_Factor of covariance parameter is not positive d 1

Those will probably go away if you set adapt_delta higher, say to 0.9, or 0.95
or 0.99. It may also help to set stepsize=0.01 or 0.1 (that's the initial
step size).

But the better way to solve the numerical issues for efficiency sake
is to use Cholesky-factor parameterizations. There's an example in the
regression chapter of the manual.

Also, this

vector[3] p; // Choice probabilities
p[1] <- exp(x1_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
p[2] <- exp(x2_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
p[3] <- exp(x3_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
#p[4] <- exp(x4_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
p <- p / sum(p);
y[n] ~ categorical(p); // Model for choice

can be more economically (in computation and lines of code) be written
by declaring x_c to replace x1_c, x2_c, and x3_c as

matrix[3, K_c] x_c[N];

then replacing all of the above with

y[n] ~ categorical_logit(x_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);

The softmax operation, exp(u) / sum(exp(u)), is built into the
categorical_logit.

- Bob

On Wednesday, October 12, 2016 at 2:18:15 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

There weren't any errors per se, just compiler warnings
and some numerical exceptions at runtime:

Exception thrown at line 34: lkj_corr_log: y is not positive definite.                                   9
Exception thrown at line 40: multi_normal_log: LDLT_Factor of covariance parameter is not positive d     1

Those will probably go away if you set adapt_delta higher, say to 0.9, or 0.95
or 0.99.  It may also help to set stepsize=0.01 or 0.1 (that's the initial
step size).

But the better way to solve the numerical issues for efficiency sake
is to use Cholesky-factor parameterizations.  There's an example in the
regression chapter of the manual.

Also, this

vector[3] p; // Choice probabilities
p[1] <- exp(x1_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
p[2] <- exp(x2_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
p[3] <- exp(x3_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
#p[4] <- exp(x4_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);
p <- p / sum(p);
y[n] ~ categorical(p); // Model for choice

can be more economically (in computation and lines of code) be written
by declaring x_c to replace x1_c, x2_c, and x3_c as

  matrix[3, K_c] x_c[N];

then replacing all of the above with

  y[n] ~ categorical_logit(x_c[n] * beta[r[n]]);

The softmax operation,  exp(u) / sum(exp(u)),  is built into the
categorical_logit.

Daniel

On Thursday, October 13, 2016 at 4:51:53 AM UTC-4, dg wrote:

Hi Krishna,

As mentioned before, I (Daniel Guhl) work together with Sebastian Gabel on Stan programs for similar models. Please find attached code for the MXL model that is a bit more optimized and uses typicaltricks/suggestions to improve performance (non-centered parameterization, vecotrization, lkj-priors). There might be still room for improvement (and we’re open for suggestions) but it runs fast (in terms of time per n_eff) and we don't have issues with warnings. Hence, we’re quite satisfied. BTW, we present results using this implementation today at eRum 2016 in Poznan.

PS: data in the example is taken from here: https://faculty.fuqua.duke.edu/~jch8/bio/Papers/Huber%20Train%202001%20Marketing%20Letters.pdf

PPS: Thanx to Bob Carpenter for already giving us suggestions to improve to code.

Hope this helps!

Best, 

Daniel
